_note: Original advanced lesson. Uses language-specific block variants where syntax differs.
title: Linked Lists
summary: A **linked list** is made of **nodes**. Each node stores data and a link to the next node.
refresher: A **linked list** stores **values** in **nodes**. Each node has data and a next link. The head points to the first node, and traversal follows next links until there is no next node.
refresher_code:
node = data + next
head -> first node

advanced-node-parts.title: A node has data and a next link
advanced-node-parts.body: The data is the **value**. The next link points to the following **node**.
advanced-node-parts.notice: The **list** order comes from links, not from **array** positions.
advanced-node-parts.mistake: Changing a link too early can lose the rest of the **list**.

advanced-head-meaning.title: Head means first node
advanced-head-meaning.body: The head **reference** points to where **traversal** starts.
advanced-head-meaning.notice: If head is null, the **list** is empty.
advanced-head-meaning.mistake: Do not treat head like a **value**. It is a **reference** to a **node**.

advanced-insert-after.title: Insert without losing the chain
advanced-insert-after.body: Point the new **node** to the old next node before changing the current node's next link.
advanced-insert-after.mistake: Assigning current.next first can disconnect the rest of the **list**.

sections.title: Node shape
sections.summary: Every **linked list** starts with the **node** idea.

blocks.body: A **linked list** does not store items side by side like an **array**. It stores small **objects** called nodes. Each node carries one value and a link to the next node.

blocks.title: Do not lose the link
blocks.caption: Watch how a new **node** is inserted between two existing nodes.

steps.title: Start with two nodes
steps.body: A points to C. Head points to A.

steps.title: Create B
steps.body: Make the new **node** before changing links.

steps.title: Point B to C
steps.body: B should remember the **node** that used to come after A.

steps.title: Point A to B
steps.body: Now A can point to B. The final order is A, B, C.

blocks.title: Read the node
items: `value` is the data stored in this **node**.
`None`, `null`, or `nullptr` means there is no next **node**.
The `head` **variable** points to the first **node** in the **list**.

blocks.title: C++ pointer note
blocks.body: `Node*` means the **variable** holds the address of a **node**. `nullptr` means it points to no node right now.

blocks.why: The head is the starting **reference** for the **list**.

sections.title: Walk through a linked list
sections.summary: **Traversal** means following next links one at a time.

blocks.body: You cannot jump straight to item 10 in a basic **linked list**. You start at head, read the current **node**, then move to current.next.

blocks.title: Move current one link at a time
blocks.caption: Watch **traversal** follow next links from head until the **list** ends.

steps.title: Start at head
steps.body: current points to the first **node**, A.
steps.what_changed: **Traversal** starts from the head **reference**, not from an **index**.

steps.title: Move to next
steps.body: After reading A, current follows A.next to B.
steps.what_changed: The **pointer** moves. The **nodes** stay where they are.

steps.title: Move again
steps.body: After B, current follows B.next to C.
steps.what_changed: A **loop** repeats this same movement until next is missing.

steps.title: Stop at null
steps.body: C.next is null, so the **traversal** is done after C.
steps.what_changed: The missing link marks the end of the **list**.

state.note: loop stops when current becomes null

blocks.caption: **Traversal** keeps moving until the current **node** is missing.

python.code:
current = head
while current is not None:
    print(current.value)
    current = current.next

blocks.title: Move the pointer
blocks.body: If you forget `current = current.next`, the **loop** keeps looking at the same **node** forever.

blocks.why: The end of the **list** is marked by a missing next **node**.

sections.title: Practice with array-backed links
sections.summary: Coding Tutor linked-list practice uses arrays to model nodes safely across languages.

blocks.body: Some practice problems represent a linked list with two arrays: one for values and one for next indexes. That keeps Python, JavaScript, Java, and C++ runners consistent while still teaching head, current, next, and null.

blocks.caption: `nextIndexes[i]` tells you which node comes after index `i`. A value such as `-1` means the list ends.

python.code:
values = [10, 20, 30]
next_indexes = [1, 2, -1]
current = 0
while current != -1:
    print(values[current])
    current = next_indexes[current]

blocks.title: Follow next, not index order
blocks.body: A linked list can store node data in any array position. The next pointer decides the order, not the physical index.

blocks.prompt: In an array-backed linked list, what does `-1` usually mean?
choices: the next node is index one
blocks.why: The sentinel value marks the end, like null in a node-based linked list.

sections.title: Insert and delete by changing links
sections.summary: Linked-**list** edits are mostly careful link updates.

blocks.body: To insert after a **node**, the new node must point to the old next node. Then the current node can point to the new node.

blocks.caption: The order matters when inserting after `current`.
blocks.body: The safer version saves the old link before replacing it.
To delete the **node** after `current`, skip over it. Point `current.next` to the node after the deleted node.

python.code:
if current.next is not None:
    current.next = current.next.next

blocks.title: C++ ownership note
blocks.body: In real C++, deleting a **node** may also require freeing **memory**. The practice runner focuses on **pointer** shape first, but production code should use safe ownership patterns.

blocks.title: Insert X after A in A -> B
Delete B after A in A -> B -> C

blocks.prompt: Why is `current.next = newNode` too early during insert?
choices: It can lose the old next node
It makes the list circular on purpose
blocks.why: Once current.next changes, you may no longer have a path to the old next **node**.
